# Cofibrations and Neighborhood Deformation Retracts in the Category of Frölicher Spaces

## Introduction and Motivation

The category of Frölicher spaces provides a natural setting in which to extend classical constructions from algebraic topology to a smooth context, encompassing manifolds, orbifolds, and a wide variety of singular spaces within a single categorical framework. A central obstacle in transferring homotopy-theoretic machinery to this setting lies in the notion of *cofibration*. The classical definition of a cofibration, formulated in terms of the homotopy extension property with respect to arbitrary continuous homotopies $H: X \times [0,1] \to Y$, does not adapt directly to the smooth category: requiring the extension of an arbitrary smooth homotopy to satisfy smoothness conditions at the boundary of the unit interval imposes constraints that are frequently too rigid to be satisfied by natural geometric examples. In particular, the sharp corners inherent in the standard parametrization of $[0,1]$ create technical difficulties when one attempts to glue or extend smooth structures across subspaces.

To circumvent this difficulty, we introduce a modified notion of cofibration for Frölicher spaces based on a *flattened* unit interval. Rather than using the interval $[0,1]$ with its usual smooth structure, we work with a reparametrized version whose derivatives vanish to infinite order at the endpoints. This flattening ensures that homotopies constructed piecewise, or extended from a subspace, automatically satisfy the necessary smoothness matching conditions at the boundary, since all derivatives of the reparametrizing function vanish there. The resulting definition of a *smooth cofibration* is formally weaker than a naive transcription of the classical homotopy extension property, yet it retains enough structure to support the fundamental constructions of homotopy theory—mapping cylinders, cofiber sequences, and the associated exact sequences—within the smooth category. This weakening is essential: it is precisely what permits smooth homotopy extensions to be constructed in situations where the classical, unflattened definition would fail to apply.

## Cofibrations and Neighborhood Deformation Retracts

Having established this notion of smooth cofibration, the paper proceeds to investigate its relationship to the concept of a *smooth neighborhood deformation retract* (NDR). Recall that in classical topology, a closed subspace $A$ of a space $X$ is a neighborhood deformation retract if there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $A$ in $X$ together with a deformation retraction of $U$ onto $A$, subject to compatibility conditions relating the retraction to the inclusion. The Frölicher-space analogue of this notion requires that the deformation retraction, together with the associated structure maps, be smooth in the sense appropriate to the category of Frölicher spaces.

The central technical result of the paper establishes a precise correspondence between these two notions. Specifically, it is shown that a closed Frölicher subspace $A \subseteq X$ is a smooth neighborhood deformation retract of $X$ if and only if the inclusion map
$$
i : A \hookrightarrow X
$$
belongs to a distinguished subclass of the smooth cofibrations defined above. This subclass is characterized by additional compatibility conditions—beyond the basic homotopy extension property—that ensure the existence of the requisite tubular neighborhood structure and retraction data. Thus the abstract, homotopy-theoretic property of being a cofibration is shown to be equivalent, for closed inclusions satisfying this refined condition, to the more geometric property of admitting a smooth deformation retraction from a neighborhood.

This result is significant both structurally and practically. Structurally, it demonstrates that the flattened-interval definition of cofibration is not merely a technical convenience but captures a geometrically meaningful class of inclusions, tightly linked to the existence of tubular neighborhood-type structures in the smooth category. Practically, it furnishes a criterion, more tractable in explicit examples, for verifying that a given inclusion of Frölicher spaces is a smooth NDR, by reducing the verification to the (often more accessible) task of checking the cofibration property.

## Relation to Classical Algebraic Topology

The characterization obtained here should be viewed as a direct smooth analogue of a well-known result in classical algebraic topology, wherein cofibrations of topological spaces satisfying appropriate closedness and normality conditions are shown to coincide with closed neighborhood deformation retracts. In the classical setting, this equivalence underlies much of the technical apparatus used to construct CW approximations, to verify the homotopy extension property in concrete examples such as CW pairs and manifold pairs, and to establish the well-definedness of various homotopy-theoretic invariants. The result established in this paper transports this equivalence, suitably reinterpreted, into the category of Frölicher spaces, thereby confirming that the flattened-interval definition of cofibration is the "correct" smooth analogue of the classical notion: it recovers, in the appropriate sense, the same relationship to neighborhood deformation retracts that one observes classically. This correspondence lends further credibility to the overall framework, suggesting that the machinery of smooth cofibrations developed here is a faithful and useful transcription of classical cofibration theory to the smooth setting, rather than an ad hoc modification tailored only to isolated examples.

## Application: The Right Puppe Sequence

As a substantial application demonstrating the utility of this theory, the paper constructs the *right Puppe sequence* within the category of Frölicher spaces. In classical topology, the Puppe sequence associated to a cofibration $i: A \hookrightarrow X$ is the sequence
$$
A \xrightarrow{\ i\ } X \xrightarrow{\ q\ } X/A \to \Sigma A \to \Sigma X \to \Sigma(X/A) \to \cdots,
$$
obtained by iterating the cofiber construction and using the suspension functor, and it plays a foundational role in stable and unstable homotopy theory, underlying long exact sequences in generalized cohomology theories and the construction of fiber and cofiber sequences more generally.

The construction of this sequence in the Frölicher setting requires precisely the homotopy extension property guaranteed by the smooth cofibration structure established earlier: at each stage of the construction, one must extend a smooth homotopy from a subspace to the ambient space, and it is exactly this extension property—rendered available by the flattened-interval definition of cofibration—that permits the iterative construction to proceed smoothly, in both the topological and differential sense. The resulting right Puppe sequence provides a foundational tool for developing a genuinely smooth homotopy theory of Frölicher spaces, opening the way to smooth analogues of cofiber sequences, generalized cohomology theories, and related exact sequence machinery, all within a category rich enough to include smooth manifolds, orbifolds, and many singular spaces of geometric interest.

# Smooth Cofibrations, Neighborhood Deformation Retracts, and the Puppe Sequence in the Category of Frölicher Spaces

## Introduction and Motivation

The category $\mathsf{FS}$ of Frölicher spaces provides a convenient setting in which to do differential geometry and smooth homotopy theory outside the restrictive framework of finite-dimensional manifolds. A Frölicher space $X$ consists of a set equipped with a compatible pair $(C,\mathcal{F})$ of a family of curves $C \subseteq \mathrm{Map}(\mathbb{R},X)$ and a family of real-valued functions $\mathcal{F}\subseteq \mathrm{Map}(X,\mathbb{R})$, satisfying the usual saturation conditions: a curve $c$ belongs to $C$ if and only if $f\circ c$ is smooth for every $f\in\mathcal{F}$, and a function $f$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}$ if and only if $f\circ c$ is smooth for every $c\in C$. This structure is flexible enough to include manifolds, infinite-dimensional manifolds, orbifolds, and many singular spaces, while still supporting a robust notion of smooth map.

A recurring obstacle in extending classical homotopy-theoretic constructions to $\mathsf{FS}$ is that the naive transcription of topological definitions frequently fails to interact well with the smooth structure. This is particularly evident for the notion of a *cofibration*. Classically, a map $i: A \to X$ is a cofibration if it satisfies the homotopy extension property (HEP) with respect to the unit interval $[0,1]$: given a homotopy $H: A\times[0,1]\to Y$ and a map $f: X\to Y$ agreeing with $H$ at time $0$ along $i$, there exists an extension of $H$ to $X\times[0,1]$. When one attempts to reproduce this definition verbatim in $\mathsf{FS}$, using the standard smooth interval $[0,1]$ with its usual Frölicher structure, the resulting notion of cofibration turns out to be too rigid: the corner behavior of $[0,1]$ at its endpoints, together with the strict differentiability requirements imposed by the Frölicher structure, obstructs the existence of smooth extensions in many natural geometric situations where one would expect a cofibration-like property to hold. In particular, closed embeddings of submanifolds — which classically are always cofibrations — need not satisfy the naive smooth HEP.

## Flattening the Unit Interval and Smooth Cofibrations

To remedy this, we introduce a modified interval object better suited to the smooth category. Let $\overline{[0,1]}$ denote the *flattened unit interval*, that is, the Frölicher space with underlying set $[0,1]$ whose structure is generated by curves that are flat (infinitely tangent to a constant) at $t=0$ and $t=1$ to all orders. More precisely, we declare a curve $c:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$ to be a generating curve of $\overline{[0,1]}$ if $c$ is smooth in the usual sense and moreover satisfies $c^{(n)}(t) = 0$ for all $n\geq 1$ whenever $c(t)\in\{0,1\}$. This flattening absorbs the corner singularities that obstruct extension: smooth maps out of $A\times \overline{[0,1]}$ automatically vanish to infinite order in the "time" direction near the ends, which provides exactly the flexibility needed to glue a homotopy on $A \times \overline{[0,1]}$ with a given map on $X \times \{0\}$ into a single smooth map on $X\times\overline{[0,1]}$.

With this modified interval in hand, we define: a smooth map $i: A\to X$ in $\mathsf{FS}$ is a **smooth cofibration** if it has the homotopy extension property with respect to $\overline{[0,1]}$, i.e., for every Frölicher space $Y$, every smooth map $f:X\to Y$, and every smooth homotopy $H: A\times \overline{[0,1]} \to Y$ with $H(-,0) = f\circ i$, there exists a smooth map $\widetilde H: X\times\overline{[0,1]}\to Y$ extending both $f$ and $H$ appropriately. We show that this weakened notion is considerably better behaved than its naive counterpart: it is closed under pushout along smooth maps, composition, and satisfies a smooth analogue of the standard cofibration recognition lemmas, while still specializing correctly on manifolds to detect the geometrically expected class of embeddings.

## Smooth Neighborhood Deformation Retracts

In parallel, we study a local geometric counterpart of the cofibration condition. A closed Frölicher subspace $A\subseteq X$ is called a **smooth neighborhood deformation retract (SNDR)** of $X$ if there exists an open neighborhood $U$ of $A$ in $X$ together with a smooth homotopy
$$ r: U\times \overline{[0,1]} \to X $$
such that $r(-,0) = \mathrm{id}_U$, $r(-,1)$ maps $U$ into $A$, and $r(a,t) = a$ for all $a\in A$ and all $t\in \overline{[0,1]}$. This is the natural smooth analogue of the classical notion of a neighborhood deformation retract familiar from algebraic topology, again formulated using the flattened interval so that the deformation retraction is compatible with the Frölicher smooth structure near the boundary times $t=0,1$.

## Main Result

The principal theorem of the paper establishes the expected bridge between the local geometric condition (SNDR) and the global homotopical condition (smooth cofibration), while pinpointing exactly which subclass of smooth cofibrations corresponds to it:

> **Theorem.** Let $A$ be a closed Frölicher subspace of a Frölicher space $X$. Then $A$ is a smooth neighborhood deformation retract of $X$ if and only if the inclusion $i: A\hookrightarrow X$ is a *closed smooth cofibration* — that is, a smooth cofibration in the above sense which is additionally a closed embedding satisfying the appropriate local triviality/normal-tube condition near $A$.

The proof proceeds along two main lines. First, given the SNDR data $(U,r)$, one constructs the required extensions demanded by the smooth HEP by first retracting into $A$ using $r$ and the flattened interval structure, and then invoking the extension over $A$; the flatness of curves at the endpoints of $\overline{[0,1]}$ ensures that the resulting homotopies patch together smoothly across $U$ and $X\setminus A$. Conversely, given that $i$ is a closed smooth cofibration, one applies the smooth HEP to the tautological homotopy on $A\times\overline{[0,1]}$ collapsing $A$ to itself, using the identity map of $X$ as the initial data, to produce a smooth retraction of a neighborhood of $A$ onto $A$; the flattened interval again guarantees that the retracting homotopy so produced is smooth in the sense required by the Frölicher structure, and a partition-of-unity-free gluing argument (adapted to the Frölicher setting via the function-based description of smoothness) shows that this retraction can be arranged to satisfy the SNDR conditions exactly.

## Application: The Right Puppe Sequence

This characterization is not merely of independent geometric interest; it is precisely the technical input needed to construct the **right Puppe sequence** in $\mathsf{FS}$. Recall that in classical homotopy theory, the existence of the Puppe sequence
$$ A \xrightarrow{i} X \to X/A \to \Sigma A \to \Sigma X \to \cdots $$
associated to a cofibration $i:A\to X$ relies crucially on the fact that cofibrations are, up to homotopy, equivalent to inclusions of neighborhood deformation retracts, so that the mapping cone construction and its iterated suspensions behave correctly with respect to smooth homotopy equivalence. Using the theorem above, we show that whenever $A\hookrightarrow X$ is a closed smooth cofibration, the smooth mapping cone $C_i = X\cup_A CA$ (formed using the smooth cone built from $\overline{[0,1]}$) fits into a sequence of smooth cofibrations
$$ A \to X \to C_i \to C_{i}/X \to \cdots $$
which, upon passing to smooth homotopy classes of maps into an arbitrary Frölicher space $Y$, yields the expected long exact Puppe sequence of smooth homotopy sets (and groups, once one reaches the smooth suspensions). The SNDR characterization is used at each stage to verify that the relevant quotient maps appearing in the sequence are again closed smooth cofibrations, which is the key inductive step allowing the construction to be iterated indefinitely.

## Outline

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls the necessary background on Frölicher spaces and introduces the flattened interval $\overline{[0,1]}$ in detail, establishing its basic categorical properties. Section 3 defines smooth cofibrations and develops their formal properties, including stability under pushout and composition. Section 4 introduces smooth neighborhood deformation retracts and proves the main characterization theorem. Section 5 applies these results to construct the smooth mapping cone and the right Puppe sequence, and discusses examples, including embeddings of finite-dimensional submanifolds and inclusions arising from smooth partitions of unity on Frölicher spaces.

# Cofibrations and the Puppe Sequence

In algebraic topology, cofibrations play a fundamental role in the study of homotopy theory, particularly through their connection to the Puppe sequence, a construction named after the mathematician Dieter Puppe.

## Cofibrations

A map $i: A \to X$ is called a **cofibration** if it satisfies the homotopy extension property (HEP). This means that for any space $Y$, given a homotopy $H: A \times I \to Y$ and a map $f: X \to Y$ that agrees with $H$ at time $0$ on $A$, there exists an extension of $H$ to a homotopy $\tilde{H}: X \times I \to Y$ that extends $f$. Intuitively, cofibrations allow homotopies defined on a subspace to be extended to the whole space.

A classical example of a cofibration is the inclusion of a CW-subcomplex $A$ into a CW-complex $X$. More generally, any inclusion of a closed subspace that is a neighborhood deformation retract tends to be a cofibration.

## The Puppe Sequence

Given a cofibration $i: A \to X$, one can form the **mapping cone** $C_i = X \cup_A CA$, obtained by attaching the cone on $A$ to $X$ along $i$. This construction leads naturally to a sequence of spaces and maps:

$$A \xrightarrow{i} X \xrightarrow{j} C_i \xrightarrow{k} C_i/X \xrightarrow{} \cdots$$

Iterating this cone construction produces the **Puppe sequence**:

$$A \to X \to C_i \to C_j \to C_k \to \cdots$$

A key feature of this sequence is that consecutive maps behave like cofibrations up to homotopy, and applying any homotopy functor (such as a generalized cohomology theory) to the Puppe sequence yields a **long exact sequence**. This is one of the most powerful applications of the construction: it provides a systematic way to derive long exact sequences in homotopy and (co)homology theories from a single cofibration.

## Significance

The Puppe sequence generalizes the exact sequence of a pair in singular homology and connects deeply with the theory of fibrations through Eckmann–Hilton duality. While cofibrations and the mapping cone construction produce the Puppe sequence, the dual notion—fibrations and the mapping path space—produces an analogous exact sequence in homotopy groups, known as the **fiber sequence**.

Together, these dual constructions form a cornerstone of modern homotopy theory, providing essential tools for computing invariants and understanding the categorical structure underlying spaces and their maps.

Classical cofibration theory, rooted in the category of topological spaces, characterizes cofibrations via the homotopy extension property (HEP) with respect to continuous homotopies. When passing to the category of Frölicher spaces—a convenient setting for generalized smooth structures that subsumes manifolds, orbifolds, and infinite-dimensional smooth spaces—the standard cofibration axioms prove overly restrictive, as they implicitly presuppose a compatibility between the extension property and topological (rather than smooth) structure maps.
